records.source: וְאֵ֨לֶּה֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י הַסֵּ֔פֶר אֲשֶׁ֥ר שָׁלַ֛ח יִרְמְיָ֥ה הַנָּבִ֖יא מִירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם אֶל־יֶ֜תֶר זִקְנֵ֣י הַגּוֹלָ֗ה וְאֶל־הַכֹּהֲנִ֤ים וְאֶל־הַנְּבִיאִים֙ וְאֶל־כָּל־הָעָ֔ם אֲשֶׁ֨ר הֶגְלָ֧ה נְבֽוּכַדְנֶאצַּ֛ר מִירוּשָׁלִַ֖ם בָּבֶֽלָה׃
records.gloss: And these [are the] words of the letter that sent Jeremiah the prophet from Jerusalem to [the] rest of [the] elders of the exile, and to the priests and to the prophets and to all the people whom had exiled Nebuchadnezzar from Jerusalem to Babylon,
pieces: This is the text of the letter Jeremiah the prophet sent from Jerusalem to the elders who were left among the exiles, to the priests and the prophets, and to all the people Nebuchadnezzar had carried into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon,

L.1: And these [are] the words of the letter that Jeremiah the prophet sent from Jerusalem to the rest of the elders of the exiles, and to the priests and to the prophets and to all the people whom Nebuchadnezzar had exiled from Jerusalem to Babylon,

R.1: This is the letter that Jeremiah the prophet sent from Jerusalem to the people who had been taken away to Babylon as captives. He wrote to the elders among them who were still alive, to the priests and the prophets, and to all the other people Nebuchadnezzar had taken from Jerusalem to Babylon.

decisions.choice: the letter: a written message sent from Jerusalem to the exiles in Babylon, some years after 597 BC
decisions.reason: The word means a written document, here a letter (2 Samuel 11:14; 2 Kings 5:5). Jeremiah stayed in Jerusalem, so he sent God's word to the exiles in writing. The letter is not dated; it was sent after the exile of 597 BC (verse 2) in the reign of Zedekiah (verse 3), and it belongs with the events of chapters 27-28, which are set early in that reign.

decisions.choice: the rest of the elders: the elders who were still living, or who remained
decisions.reason: The word means what is left over. It may simply mean the elders who were there, or it may hint that some had died on the journey or since, or had been put to death (compare verses 21-22). The text does not say which.

decisions.choice: the exile: the exiles as one group
decisions.reason: The noun means "exile" and is used for the whole company of those taken away, as in 24:5.

decisions.choice: Nebuchadnezzar: the form of the name with n
decisions.reason: Chapters 27-29 mostly spell the Babylonian king's name Nebuchadnezzar, as Kings does; most of Jeremiah spells it Nebuchadrezzar, and this chapter has that form in verse 21. Both name the same king (see 25:1).

decisions.choice: the chapter's place in the Greek translation
decisions.reason: In the Greek translation (the Septuagint) this chapter is numbered 36, since the oracles against the nations come earlier there (see 1:1 and 25:13), and it is shorter: it lacks verses 16-20 and parts of other verses (see verses 14 and 16). The Hebrew is followed.

decisions.choice: Nebuchadnezzar
decisions.reason: Each verse keeps the form of the king's name its Hebrew uses (m4).

decisions.choice: the elders who were left among the exiles (Balanced); the elders among them who were still alive (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "the rest of the elders" means in ordinary English. Readable splits the verse into two sentences and calls the exiles "people taken away as captives".

records.heading: A letter to the people in exile

records.source: אַחֲרֵ֣י צֵ֣את יְכָנְיָֽה־הַ֠מֶּלֶךְ וְהַגְּבִירָ֨ה וְהַסָּרִיסִ֜ים שָׂרֵ֨י יְהוּדָ֧ה וִירוּשָׁלִַ֛ם וְהֶחָרָ֥שׁ וְהַמַּסְגֵּ֖ר מִירוּשָׁלִָֽם׃
records.gloss: after went out Jeconiah the king and the queen mother and the eunuchs, [the] princes of Judah and Jerusalem, and the craftsman and the smith from Jerusalem,
pieces: after King Jeconiah, the queen mother, the court officers, the officials of Judah and Jerusalem, and the craftsmen and smiths had gone from Jerusalem into exile,

L.2: after Jeconiah the king and the queen mother and the eunuchs, the princes of Judah and Jerusalem, and the craftsmen and the smiths had gone out from Jerusalem,

R.2: This was after King Jeconiah had been taken away from Jerusalem. The king's mother, the palace officials, the leaders of Judah and Jerusalem, and the skilled workers and metalworkers had been taken with him.

decisions.choice: went out: left the city in surrender and went into exile
decisions.reason: Jeconiah went out of the besieged city to the king of Babylon and gave himself up, and he and his court were carried off (2 Kings 24:12, 15).

decisions.choice: the queen mother: the king's mother, who held an honored place at court
decisions.reason: The title means "great lady". The king's mother had a rank of her own (13:18; 22:26; 1 Kings 2:19). Jeconiah's mother was Nehushta (2 Kings 24:8), and she was taken to Babylon with him (2 Kings 24:12, 15).

decisions.choice: the eunuchs: royal court officials, perhaps castrated men
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 24:12, the word names a class of court officers. Many such officers in the courts of the ancient Near East were castrated, but the word is also used of high officials who were not.

decisions.choice: the same groups as in 2 Kings 24:12-16 and Jeremiah 24:1
decisions.reason: Kings lists the king, his mother, his servants, princes and eunuchs, the leading men, the warriors, the craftsmen and the smiths (2 Kings 24:12-16); Jeremiah 24:1 names the same king, the princes and the two trades. Jeconiah is the king called Jehoiachin in Kings and Coniah in 22:24. The princes are here called "of Judah and Jerusalem".

decisions.choice: eunuchs, princes (Literal); court officers, officials (Balanced); palace officials, leaders (Readable); craftsmen and smiths (Readable: skilled workers and metalworkers)
decisions.reason: Worded as in 2 Kings 24:12-16. Balanced uses "officials" for the princes, as usual in these books, so it calls the eunuchs "court officers" to keep the two groups apart; Readable has "leaders" and "palace officials".

decisions.choice: had gone from Jerusalem into exile (Balanced); had been taken away (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "went out" meant here (m1). Readable starts a new sentence and says "with him" for the list of those taken.

records.source: בְּיַד֙ אֶלְעָשָׂ֣ה בֶן־שָׁפָ֔ן וּגְמַרְיָ֖ה בֶּן־חִלְקִיָּ֑ה אֲשֶׁ֨ר שָׁלַ֜ח צִדְקִיָּ֣ה מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֗ה אֶל־נְבוּכַדְנֶאצַּ֛ר מֶ֥לֶךְ בָּבֶ֖ל בָּבֶ֥לָה לֵאמֹֽר׃ס
records.gloss: by [the] hand of Elasah son of Shaphan and Gemariah son of Hilkiah, whom sent Zedekiah king of Judah to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon [to] Babylon, saying:
pieces: sending it by Elasah son of Shaphan and Gemariah son of Hilkiah. Zedekiah king of Judah had sent these two men to Babylon, to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. The letter said:

L.3: by the hand of Elasah son of Shaphan and Gemariah son of Hilkiah, whom Zedekiah king of Judah sent to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, to Babylon, saying:

R.3: Jeremiah gave the letter to Elasah son of Shaphan and Gemariah son of Hilkiah. Zedekiah king of Judah was sending them to Babylon to see Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. The letter said:

decisions.choice: by the hand of: carried by
decisions.reason: To send something "by the hand of" someone is to have that person carry it. The two men were travelling to Babylon on the king's business and took Jeremiah's letter with them.

decisions.choice: Elasah son of Shaphan: probably of the family that supported Jeremiah
decisions.reason: Shaphan was King Josiah's scribe (2 Kings 22:3-14). His son Ahikam protected Jeremiah when his life was in danger (26:24), and another son, Gemariah, and a grandson heard Baruch's scroll and tried to keep it from being burned (36:10-12, 25). Elasah is probably another of Shaphan's sons, though the text does not say so.

decisions.choice: Gemariah son of Hilkiah: a different man from Gemariah son of Shaphan
decisions.reason: This Gemariah is not the son of Shaphan in 36:10. His father Hilkiah may be the high priest who found the book of the law under Josiah (2 Kings 22:4-8), but the name was common, and Jeremiah's own father was a Hilkiah (1:1).

decisions.choice: whom Zedekiah sent to Nebuchadnezzar: envoys of a king who ruled under Babylon
decisions.reason: Nebuchadnezzar had made Zedekiah king (2 Kings 24:17), and Zedekiah owed him loyalty and tribute. The text does not say why he sent these men, perhaps to pay tribute or to assure the king of his loyalty after the talk of revolt in chapter 27. Zedekiah himself went, or sent an officer, to Babylon in his fourth year (51:59).

decisions.choice: saying: the letter follows, from verse 4 to verse 23
decisions.reason: The word introduces the words of the letter. It is God's message, set out as "Thus says the LORD", and it ends at verse 23.

decisions.choice: The letter said:
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable introduce the letter with a short sentence of its own. Balanced continues the sentence with "sending it by"; Readable starts new sentences and says that the envoys were going "to see" the king.

records.source: כֹּ֥ה אָמַ֛ר יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל לְכָל־הַ֨גּוֹלָ֔ה אֲשֶׁר־הִגְלֵ֥יתִי מִירוּשָׁלִַ֖ם בָּבֶֽלָה׃
records.gloss: Thus says Yahweh of hosts, [the] God of Israel, to all the exile whom I exiled from Jerusalem to Babylon:
pieces: "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies, the God of Israel, says this to all the exiles whom I sent into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon:

L.4: "Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of hosts, the God of Israel, to all the exiles whom I have exiled from Jerusalem to Babylon:

R.4: "This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies, the God of Israel, says to all the people I sent away from Jerusalem to Babylon as captives:

decisions.choice: whom I have exiled: the exile was God's own act
decisions.reason: Verse 1 says that Nebuchadnezzar exiled them; here God says that he himself did it. Babylon was the instrument of his judgment, and the same God will bring them back (verses 10-14; 24:5).

decisions.choice: the letter speaks in God's voice from here to verse 23
decisions.reason: The letter is Jeremiah's, but its words are God's, spoken in the first person. The quotation of the letter runs to the end of verse 23.

decisions.choice: Thus says the LORD of hosts (Literal); The LORD of Armies ... says this (Balanced); This is what the LORD of Armies ... says (Readable)
decisions.reason: The wording set for this formula in Isaiah and Jeremiah (see Isaiah 1:9 on "hosts").

decisions.choice: an opening quotation mark
decisions.reason: The letter is quoted, so it opens with a quotation mark here and closes at the end of verse 23. God's words inside it take no further marks, as in 7:3.

records.source: בְּנ֥וּ בָתִּ֖ים וְשֵׁ֑בוּ וְנִטְע֣וּ גַנּ֔וֹת וְאִכְל֖וּ אֶת־פִּרְיָֽן׃
records.gloss: Build houses and dwell, and plant gardens and eat their produce.
pieces: Build houses and settle down in them. Plant gardens and eat what they produce.

L.5: Build houses and live [in them]; and plant gardens and eat their produce.

R.5: Build houses and live in them. Plant gardens and eat the food they grow.

decisions.choice: build and live, plant and eat: the curse of Deuteronomy 28:30 turned around
decisions.reason: Moses warned that if Israel broke the covenant they would build houses and not live in them, and plant vineyards and not enjoy their fruit (Deuteronomy 28:30, 39). In exile, the very place of that curse, God tells his people to build and live, plant and eat. The verbs "build" and "plant" also recall Jeremiah's call (1:10).

decisions.choice: live: settle and stay
decisions.reason: The verb means to sit, to dwell, to stay. With "build houses" it means to make a settled home, not to wait for a quick return; verse 28 sums the advice up as "It will be long".

decisions.choice: gardens: plots of vegetables and fruit trees
decisions.reason: A garden was an enclosed plot of fruit trees and vegetables. Planting one meant waiting for years of harvests.

decisions.choice: [in them] (Literal); settle down in them (Balanced)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says only "dwell"; English needs to say where. Balanced says "settle down" to bring out m2.

records.source: קְח֣וּ נָשִׁ֗ים וְהוֹלִידוּ֮ בָּנִ֣ים וּבָנוֹת֒ וּקְח֨וּ לִבְנֵיכֶ֜ם נָשִׁ֗ים וְאֶת־בְּנֽוֹתֵיכֶם֙ תְּנ֣וּ לַֽאֲנָשִׁ֔ים וְתֵלַ֖דְנָה בָּנִ֣ים וּבָנ֑וֹת וּרְבוּ־שָׁ֖ם וְאַל־תִּמְעָֽטוּ׃
records.gloss: Take wives and father sons and daughters, and take for your sons wives, and your daughters give to husbands, and they will bear sons and daughters; and multiply there, and not become few.
pieces: Marry and have sons and daughters. Find wives for your sons and give your daughters to husbands, so that they in turn have sons and daughters. Increase in number there; do not decrease.

L.6: Take wives and father sons and daughters, and take wives for your sons and give your daughters to husbands, so that they may bear sons and daughters; and multiply there, and do not become few.

R.6: Get married and have children. Find wives for your sons and husbands for your daughters, so that they also have children. Grow in number there. Do not let your numbers get smaller.

decisions.choice: multiply there: the blessing of increase, even in exile
decisions.reason: "Be fruitful and multiply" is the blessing given at creation and after the flood (Genesis 1:28; 9:1), and Israel multiplied in Egypt even while it was oppressed (Exodus 1:7, 12). The exile is not to be the end of the people; they are to grow in number until God brings them back.

decisions.choice: take wives for your sons, give your daughters to husbands: parents arranged their children's marriages
decisions.reason: Fathers arranged marriages for their sons and daughters (Genesis 24:3-4; 34:8-9). The command reaches two generations: the exiles' grandchildren will be born in Babylon, which agrees with the seventy years of verse 10.

decisions.choice: and they will bear: so that they may bear
decisions.reason: The verb continues the commands and gives their purpose or result: the daughters given in marriage will in turn have children.

decisions.choice: Marry (Balanced); have children (Readable)
decisions.reason: "Take wives" is the Hebrew way of saying "marry". Readable says "children" for "sons and daughters", which means the same.

records.source: וְדִרְשׁ֞וּ אֶת־שְׁל֣וֹם הָעִ֗יר אֲשֶׁ֨ר הִגְלֵ֤יתִי אֶתְכֶם֙ שָׁ֔מָּה וְהִתְפַּֽלְל֥וּ בַעֲדָ֖הּ אֶל־יְהוָ֑ה כִּ֣י בִשְׁלוֹמָ֔הּ יִהְיֶ֥ה לָכֶ֖ם שָׁלֽוֹם׃פ
records.gloss: And seek [the] peace of the city where I exiled you there, and pray on its behalf to Yahweh, for in its peace will be to you peace.
pieces: Seek the peace of the city where I have sent you as exiles, and pray to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} for it, since your own peace depends on its peace.

L.7: And seek the peace of the city where I have exiled you, and pray to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} on its behalf, for in its peace there will be peace for you.

R.7: Work for the well-being of the city where I have sent you as captives. Pray to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} for it. If the city is at peace and doing well, you will be too.

decisions.choice: peace: the city's whole well-being, its safety, order and prosperity
decisions.reason: The word means wholeness and well-being of every kind: safety from war, order, health and plenty, as well as good relations between people. The exiles are to seek all of this for the city they live in. The word comes three times, so that the city's well-being and the exiles' own are bound together. Jeremiah has spoken against prophets who promised "peace" to Jerusalem when there was none (6:14; 8:11; 14:13); here God himself tells the exiles to seek it for Babylon.

decisions.choice: pray to the LORD for it: prayer for the city of the conquerors
decisions.reason: The exiles are told to pray for a foreign city, the seat of the empire that had taken them captive. This is not the same as giving up hope of return (verses 10-14). Other exiles cried out against Babylon (Psalm 137:8-9); this letter tells them to pray for its good while they live there.

decisions.choice: seek: work for, actively pursue
decisions.reason: The verb means to seek, to inquire after, to care for. It is the same verb used for seeking God in verse 13: they are to seek the good of the city and seek the LORD.

decisions.choice: the city where I have exiled you: wherever the exiles live
decisions.reason: The singular may mean Babylon itself or each town where exiles were settled; Ezekiel lived among exiles at Tel-abib by the river Chebar (Ezekiel 3:15). God again calls himself the one who exiled them (verse 4).

decisions.choice: peace (all three times)
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep the settled word "peace" and use it all three times, so the link between the city's peace and the exiles' peace stays visible; m1 says how wide the word is.

decisions.choice: well-being; at peace and doing well; you will be too
decisions.reason: Readable says "well-being" first, so that readers do not take the word to mean only the absence of war, and then puts the link between the city and the exiles in a plain "if ... then" sentence.

records.source: כִּי֩ כֹ֨ה אָמַ֜ר יְהוָ֤ה צְבָאוֹת֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אַל־יַשִּׁ֧יאוּ לָכֶ֛ם נְבִֽיאֵיכֶ֥ם אֲשֶׁר־בְּקִרְבְּכֶ֖ם וְקֹֽסְמֵיכֶ֑ם וְאַֽל־תִּשְׁמְעוּ֙ אֶל־חֲלֹמֹ֣תֵיכֶ֔ם אֲשֶׁ֥ר אַתֶּ֖ם מַחְלְמִֽים׃
records.gloss: For thus says Yahweh of hosts, [the] God of Israel: Not let deceive you your prophets who [are] in your midst and your diviners, and not listen to your dreams which you [are] causing to dream.
pieces: For {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies, the God of Israel, says this: Do not let the prophets and the diviners who are among you deceive you, and do not listen to the dreams that you urge them to dream.

L.8: For thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of hosts, the God of Israel: Do not let your prophets who [are] among you and your diviners deceive you, and do not listen to your dreams, which you are causing [them] to dream.

R.8: This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies, the God of Israel, says: Do not let the prophets and the fortune-tellers among you fool you. Do not listen to the dreams that you want them to dream for you.

decisions.choice: your prophets and your diviners: the prophets the people chose and listened to
decisions.reason: "Your" prophets are those the people themselves follow, not men God has sent (verse 9; 27:9). Diviners tried to learn the future by signs and omens, a practice the law forbids (Deuteronomy 18:10-14). Putting the two side by side shows what these prophets really were.

decisions.choice: deceive: lead astray with false hopes
decisions.reason: The verb means to deceive or delude. It is the word the Assyrian envoy used when he warned Jerusalem not to let Hezekiah deceive them (2 Kings 18:29; Isaiah 36:14), and the word Jeremiah used when he accused God of letting the people be deceived by promises of peace (4:10).

decisions.choice: the dreams which you are causing to dream: dreams the people prompt others to have
decisions.reason: The verb form is causative: "which you cause to be dreamed". It seems to mean that the people's own wishes encourage the prophets to dream what they want to hear. Some take the form as an unusual way of saying "which you dream", which would make the dreams the people's own. The sense of the warning is the same: they are not to trust dreams that tell them what they want.

decisions.choice: dreams: a recognized way of receiving a message from God
decisions.reason: God could speak in dreams (Numbers 12:6; Genesis 37:5-11), but Jeremiah sets the lying dreams of the prophets against the word of the LORD (23:25-32; 27:9).

decisions.choice: the prophets and the diviners who are among you
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the two groups together, as English does, rather than splitting them as the Hebrew does. Readable says "fortune-tellers" for the diviners and "fool" for "deceive".

decisions.choice: that you urge them to dream (Balanced); that you want them to dream for you (Readable)
decisions.reason: Literal brackets "them"; Balanced and Readable say how the people cause the dreams, as m3 reads the verb.

records.source: כִּ֣י בְשֶׁ֔קֶר הֵ֛ם נִבְּאִ֥ים לָכֶ֖ם בִּשְׁמִ֑י לֹ֥א שְׁלַחְתִּ֖ים נְאֻם־יְהוָֽה׃ס
records.gloss: For with falsehood they [are] prophesying to you in my name; not I sent them, declaration of Yahweh.
pieces: For they are prophesying lies to you in {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name. I did not send them, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

L.9: For it is falsely that they are prophesying to you in {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name; I did not send them, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

R.9: They are using {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name to tell you lies. I did not send them, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: they prophesy falsely in my name; I did not send them
decisions.reason: Jeremiah brings the same charge against the prophets of peace in Jerusalem (14:14-15; 23:21, 25) and against those who told the kings not to serve Babylon (27:15). A true prophet is one whom God sends (1:7).

decisions.choice: in my name: claiming my authority
decisions.reason: To prophesy in someone's name is to speak as his messenger, with his authority. These prophets used the LORD's name for words he had not given them.

decisions.choice: declares the LORD (Literal, Balanced); says the LORD (Readable)
decisions.reason: The wording set for this formula in Isaiah and Jeremiah.

records.source: כִּֽי־כֹה֙ אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה כִּ֠י לְפִ֞י מְלֹ֧את לְבָבֶ֛ל שִׁבְעִ֥ים שָׁנָ֖ה אֶפְקֹ֣ד אֶתְכֶ֑ם וַהֲקִמֹתִ֤י עֲלֵיכֶם֙ אֶת־דְּבָרִ֣י הַטּ֔וֹב לְהָשִׁ֣יב אֶתְכֶ֔ם אֶל־הַמָּק֖וֹם הַזֶּֽה׃
records.gloss: For thus says Yahweh: For at [the] completing for Babylon [of] seventy years I will visit you, and I will establish on you my word the good, to bring back you to the place the this.
pieces: For {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says this: When Babylon's seventy years have been completed, I will come to your aid. I will keep {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} good promise to you and bring you back to this place.

L.10: For thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: When seventy years are completed for Babylon, I will visit you, and I will fulfill for you {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} good word, to bring you back to this place.

R.10: This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says: Babylon will rule for seventy years. When those years are over, I will come and help you. I will do the good thing I promised and bring you back to this place.

decisions.choice: seventy years for Babylon: the time Jeremiah had already named
decisions.reason: Jeremiah had said that the nations would serve the king of Babylon seventy years, and that after that God would punish Babylon (25:11-12). Later readers saw the promise fulfilled when the exiles returned (2 Chronicles 36:21-22; Ezra 1:1), and Daniel prayed over these words (Daniel 9:2).

decisions.choice: for Babylon: the seventy years are the time of Babylon's power
decisions.reason: The years are counted "for Babylon": the span of its rule, not the length of any one group's exile. Babylon's empire lasted from Nebuchadnezzar's victory in 605 BC to the fall of Babylon to Cyrus in 539 BC, close to seventy years; seventy is also the span of a full human life (Psalm 90:10). Either way, the exiles would not be going home soon, against what the prophets were telling them (verses 8-9; 28:3-4).

decisions.choice: I will visit you: I will turn my attention to you, here for your good
decisions.reason: The verb means to take notice of, to attend to someone. It can mean to come to help (Genesis 50:24; Exodus 4:31) or to punish (verse 32). Here it is for good, as the rest of the verse says.

decisions.choice: I will establish my good word: I will make my promise come true
decisions.reason: To "establish" a word is to carry it out (28:6; 33:14). The "good word" is God's promise of return, given in 24:6 and spelled out in the verses that follow.

decisions.choice: come to your aid (Balanced); come and help you (Readable)
decisions.reason: "Visit" in English suggests a social call; Balanced and Readable say what God's visit means here (m3).

decisions.choice: Babylon will rule for seventy years
decisions.reason: Readable says what "for Babylon" means (m2) in a sentence of its own.

records.source: כִּי֩ אָנֹכִ֨י יָדַ֜עְתִּי אֶת־הַמַּחֲשָׁבֹ֗ת אֲשֶׁ֧ר אָנֹכִ֛י חֹשֵׁ֥ב עֲלֵיכֶ֖ם נְאֻם־יְהוָ֑ה מַחְשְׁב֤וֹת שָׁלוֹם֙ וְלֹ֣א לְרָעָ֔ה לָתֵ֥ת לָכֶ֖ם אַחֲרִ֥ית וְתִקְוָֽה׃
records.gloss: For I know the plans that I [am] planning for you, declaration of Yahweh, plans of peace and not for evil, to give to you a future and hope.
pieces: For I know well what I have planned for you, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. I have planned peace for you, not disaster, so as to give you a future and a hope.

L.11: For I, I know the plans that I am planning for you, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, plans of peace and not of evil, to give you a future and a hope.

R.11: I know what I have planned for you, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. I plan to give you well-being, not trouble. I will give you a future and something to hope for.

decisions.choice: plans for you: God's purpose for the exiles as a people
decisions.reason: The "you" is plural and means the exiles of Judah as a community. The promise belongs to the setting of verse 10: after the seventy years God will bring his people back, and the plans of peace are his purpose for the nation's future. Many readers take comfort from the verse for their own lives, and it does show what kind of God he is: his final purpose for his people is good. But it is first a promise to a people in exile, not a pledge of success to each person, and some of those who first heard it would die in Babylon before it came true.

decisions.choice: the plans that I am planning: God's settled intentions
decisions.reason: The noun and the verb come from one root: "the plans I plan". Elsewhere God says that he is planning a plan of disaster against Judah (18:11; compare 49:20; 50:45). Here the same words describe a plan of peace. The participle "I am planning" shows that the plan is already in his mind.

decisions.choice: plans of peace and not of evil: plans for well-being, not for disaster
decisions.reason: "Peace" is the same word as in verse 7: wholeness and well-being. "Evil" here means harm or disaster, not moral wickedness (compare 21:10; 24:5).

decisions.choice: a future and a hope: a hopeful future
decisions.reason: The first word means what comes afterward: the end of a matter, its outcome, the future. With "hope" it may name two things, or one thing in two words: a future full of hope. The same pair is used in 31:17 ("there is hope for your future") and Proverbs 23:18.

decisions.choice: I: said twice, for emphasis
decisions.reason: The pronoun "I" is written out before both verbs, though the verb forms already say "I". The emphasis sets God's knowledge of his own plans against the prophets' claims (verses 8-9).

decisions.choice: what I have planned for you ... I have planned peace for you, not disaster
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the plans in verbs, as English often does, and starts a new sentence for the second half; "know well" carries the emphatic "I" (m5).

decisions.choice: well-being, not trouble; a future and something to hope for
decisions.reason: Readable says "well-being" for "peace", as in verse 7, and gives "hope" as a phrase young readers can follow.

records.gloss: And you will call me and come and pray to me, and I will listen to you.
pieces: Then you will call on {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}; you will come and pray to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and I will hear you.

L.12: And you will call on {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} and come and pray to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and I will listen to you.

R.12: Then you will call to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. You will come and pray to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and I will listen to you.

decisions.choice: and you will call: what will follow from God's plans
decisions.reason: The verbs carry on from verses 10-11 and describe what the people will do when God turns to them. It is not a condition laid down first; God's promise and the people's turning to him go together.

decisions.choice: you will pray to me and I will listen: the prayer of the exiles
decisions.reason: Solomon asked that when Israel was taken captive to an enemy land, and prayed to God there, God would hear and forgive them (1 Kings 8:46-50). Moses said that in exile they would turn back to God (Deuteronomy 4:29-31; 30:1-3).

decisions.choice: come: come to God in prayer
alternatives: walk, set out (on the way back)
decisions.reason: The verb "go" or "come" stands between "call" and "pray" and means coming before God; some take it as setting out on the way home, but it most likely belongs with the prayer.

decisions.choice: Then
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable show with "Then" that this follows from verses 10-11. Balanced says "hear" for the last verb, which in Hebrew is "listen" and also "answer".

records.gloss: And you will seek me and you will find, for you will seek me with all your heart.
pieces: You will seek {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} and you will find {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, when you search for {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} with all your heart.

L.13: And you will seek {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} and find [{{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}], when you seek {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} with all your heart.

R.13: You will look for {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and you will find {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} when you look for {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} with all your heart.

decisions.choice: seek and find, with all your heart: the words of Deuteronomy 4:29
decisions.reason: Moses foretold that in exile Israel would seek the LORD and find him, when they searched for him with all their heart and soul (Deuteronomy 4:29). The letter uses the same two verbs for seeking and the same "with all your heart": what Moses foretold is now about to happen.

decisions.choice: when: the condition for finding
decisions.reason: The word can mean "when", "if" or "because", as in Deuteronomy 4:29. Wholehearted seeking is the way God is found.

decisions.choice: with all your heart: with the whole mind and will
decisions.reason: The heart is the center of thought and will. To seek with all the heart is to seek with nothing held back (Deuteronomy 6:5; Jeremiah 24:7).

decisions.choice: seek, search for (Balanced); look for (Readable)
decisions.reason: Each level follows its wording of Deuteronomy 4:29 so that the echo can be heard. Literal brackets the second "me", which the Hebrew leaves out.

I will restore your fortunes and gather you from all the nations and all the places where I have driven you, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and I will bring you back to the place from which I sent you into exile.

L.14: And I will let {{deity_pronoun:myself|Myself}} be found by you, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and I will restore your fortunes, and I will gather you from all the nations and from all the places where I have driven you, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and I will bring you back to the place from which I exiled you.

R.14: I will let you find {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. I will make things good again for you. I will gather you from all the nations and all the places where I have scattered you, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. I will bring you back to the place from which I sent you away as captives.

decisions.choice: I will be found by you: I will let myself be found
decisions.reason: The verb form means that God allows himself to be found by those who seek him (Isaiah 55:6; 65:1; 1 Chronicles 28:9). Finding him is his gift, not the seeker's achievement.

decisions.choice: I will turn your captivity: I will restore your fortunes
alternatives: I will bring back your captives
decisions.reason: The phrase is literally "turn your turning". It can mean to bring back the captives, and so it was long translated "turn your captivity", but it is also used where there is no captivity (Job 42:10) and means to restore what was lost, to turn a people's lot around. In this verse both senses fit, since the captives are to be brought home.

decisions.choice: your fortunes: the form read aloud
decisions.reason: The written consonants (ketiv) have a slightly different form of the noun; the scribes marked the more usual form to be read aloud (qere). The meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: from all the nations and all the places: a scattering wider than Babylon
decisions.reason: The promise looks beyond the exiles in Babylon to all of Israel's scattered people, as Moses foretold (Deuteronomy 30:3-4; compare 23:3).

decisions.choice: the Greek has a shorter verse
decisions.reason: The Greek translation has only "and I will appear to you" and lacks the rest of the verse. The Hebrew is followed.

decisions.choice: I will let you find me
decisions.reason: Balanced turns the passive "be found by you" into an active sentence, as English prefers.

decisions.choice: make things good again for you; scattered
decisions.reason: Readable says what "restore your fortunes" means (m2) and says "scattered" for "driven".

records.gloss: For you have said: Has raised up for us Yahweh prophets [in] Babylon.
pieces: You have been saying, '{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has raised up prophets for us here in Babylon.'

L.15: For you have said, '{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has raised up prophets for us in Babylon.'

R.15: You say, '{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has given us prophets here in Babylon.'

decisions.choice: for you have said: the reason for what follows in verses 21-23
alternatives: Since you have said ... (answered in verse 16)
decisions.reason: The sentence begins "because" or "since", and the answer to it comes in verses 21-23, which name two of these prophets in Babylon and their fate. Verses 16-20 stand between, as a message about those still in Jerusalem. Some read verse 15 with verse 16 instead: since you trust these prophets, hear what the LORD says about Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: prophets in Babylon: men among the exiles who spoke in the LORD's name
decisions.reason: There were prophets among the exiles who promised a quick return (verses 8-9, 21, 24-28). Ezekiel also prophesied among the exiles from 593 BC (Ezekiel 1:1-3), but the letter speaks of the prophets the exiles trusted against Jeremiah's word.

decisions.choice: single quotation marks
decisions.reason: The exiles' words are quoted inside the letter, so they take single quotation marks.

decisions.choice: here in Babylon (Balanced, Readable); has given us (Readable)
decisions.reason: The speakers are in Babylon, so Balanced and Readable say "here". Readable says "given" for "raised up".

records.gloss: For thus says Yahweh concerning the king who sits on [the] throne of David and concerning all the people who dwell in the city the this, your brothers who not went out with you into the exile:
pieces: But {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says this about the king who sits on David's throne and about all the people who live in this city, your {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} who did not go with you into exile:

L.16: For thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} concerning the king who sits on the throne of David and concerning all the people who live in this city, your {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} who did not go out with you into exile:

R.16: But this is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says about the king who rules from David's throne, and about all the people who still live in Jerusalem, your relatives who were not taken away with you:

decisions.choice: verses 16-20 are not in the Greek translation
decisions.reason: The Greek translation goes straight from verse 15 to verse 21. Verses 16-20 repeat words found elsewhere in Jeremiah (24:8-10; 25:4), and some think they were added to the letter; others think the Greek lost them because verse 15 and verse 20 both end with "Babylon". The Hebrew is followed.

decisions.choice: the king who sits on the throne of David: Zedekiah
decisions.reason: The king still reigning in Jerusalem was Zedekiah (verse 3), who had been put on the throne by Babylon in place of Jeconiah.

decisions.choice: for: the message about Jerusalem answers the exiles' hopes
decisions.reason: The exiles' prophets said that they would soon return (verses 8-9, 15). God's word about those left in Jerusalem shows why that cannot be: the city itself and its king are under judgment, so there will be no quick return to it.

decisions.choice: your brothers: your fellow countrymen, your own people
decisions.reason: "Brothers" here means fellow members of the people of Judah, men and women, those who were not taken to Babylon in 597 BC.

decisions.choice: your brothers and sisters (gender setting)
decisions.reason: The word means all their kin who stayed behind, women as well as men, so Literal and Balanced give an inclusive default with "brothers" as the alternative. Readable says "relatives".

decisions.choice: Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Readable names the city meant by "this city", since the exiles hearing the letter were in Babylon.

records.gloss: Thus says Yahweh of hosts: Behold, I [am] sending on them the sword, the famine and the pestilence, and I will make them like the figs the horrid which not can be eaten from badness.
pieces: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies says this: I am about to send the sword, famine and plague against them, and I will make them like rotten figs, so bad that they cannot be eaten.

L.17: Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of hosts: Look, I am sending against them the sword, the famine and the pestilence, and I will make them like horrid figs that cannot be eaten because of [their] badness.

R.17: This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies says: I am going to send war, famine and disease against them. I will make them like rotten figs that are too bad to eat.

decisions.choice: thus says the LORD of hosts: the formula repeated
decisions.reason: Verse 16 began "thus says the LORD" and named those the message concerns; the formula is said again here before the message itself.

decisions.choice: like figs that cannot be eaten: the bad figs of chapter 24
decisions.reason: In the vision of the two baskets, the bad figs that could not be eaten stood for Zedekiah, his officials and those left in Jerusalem (24:2, 8). The letter applies that vision here, though it uses a different word for "bad".

decisions.choice: horrid: disgusting, rotten
decisions.reason: The word is found only here. It seems to be related to a word for something horrible or shocking (5:30; 23:14), and so means figs so spoiled that they disgust anyone who sees them.

decisions.choice: sword, famine and pestilence (Literal); sword, famine and plague (Balanced); war, famine and disease (Readable)
decisions.reason: The wording set for this triad throughout Jeremiah.

decisions.choice: rotten figs
decisions.reason: Literal says "horrid" for the rare word (m3); Balanced and Readable say "rotten", which is what such figs are.

records.gloss: And I will pursue after them with the sword, with the famine and with the pestilence, and I will make them for a horror to all [the] kingdoms of the earth, for a curse and for a desolation and for a hissing and for a reproach among all the nations where I have driven them there,
pieces: I will pursue them with sword, famine and plague, and I will make them a horror to every kingdom on earth. Among all the nations where I have driven them, they will be a name used in curses, a thing that appalls, an object of scorn and a disgrace,

L.18: And I will pursue them with the sword, with famine and with pestilence, and I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth, an execration and an appalling thing and a hissing and a reproach among all the nations where I have driven them,

R.18: I will chase after them with war, famine and disease. All the kingdoms of the earth will be horrified at what happens to them. In all the nations where I scatter them, people will use their name as a curse. People will be shocked at them, mock them and insult them.

decisions.choice: horror: the form read aloud
decisions.reason: As in 24:9, the written consonants (ketiv) put two letters of this word in a different order; the scribes marked the usual form to be read aloud (qere). Both name the same word.

decisions.choice: a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth, a curse and a reproach: the covenant warnings fulfilled
decisions.reason: Moses warned that Israel would become a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth (Deuteronomy 28:25) and a byword among the nations (Deuteronomy 28:37). Jeremiah repeats the words in 15:4, 24:9 and 34:17.

decisions.choice: an appalling thing: a desolation that stuns those who see it
decisions.reason: The word means both a ruin and the shock it causes, as in 19:8. Those who see what has happened to them will be appalled.

decisions.choice: a hissing: the sound people made at a sight of ruin, in shock and scorn
decisions.reason: Passers-by hissed or whistled at a ruined place or people, a gesture of horror and of mockery (18:16; 19:8; Lamentations 2:15).

decisions.choice: horror; an execration (Balanced: a name used in curses); an appalling thing (Balanced: a thing that appalls); hissing (Balanced: object of scorn); reproach (Balanced: disgrace); Readable in sentences
decisions.reason: The curse word follows the wording set for these lists (42:18; 44:12). "Horror" is kept for the first word, as in 24:9, so the third word, which 19:8 calls a horror, is here "an appalling thing". The hissing follows the book's wording (19:8). Readable says what each word means in sentences of its own.

decisions.choice: two sentences; the nations first in the second
decisions.reason: Balanced divides the verse into two sentences and ends with a comma, since verse 19 gives the reason. Readable uses short sentences and says "scatter" for "drive".

pieces: because they have not listened to {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} words, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the words I sent them through {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} servants the prophets, again and again. And you did not listen either, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

L.19: because they did not listen to {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} words, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, which I sent to them by {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} servants the prophets, rising early and sending; and you did not listen, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

R.19: This is because they would not listen to {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} words, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. Over and over I sent {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} servants the prophets to them with {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} message. And you exiles did not listen either, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: rising early and sending: sending again and again, without giving up
decisions.reason: As in 7:13 and 7:25, the phrase pictures someone who starts work early each day and keeps at it.

decisions.choice: my servants the prophets: those who served God by bringing his word
decisions.reason: As in 7:25, the title honors the prophets as God's messengers (25:4; 26:5; 35:15).

decisions.choice: and you did not listen: the exiles too
decisions.reason: The verse speaks first of those in Jerusalem ("they") and then turns to the exiles hearing the letter ("you"). The exiles had not listened either, which is why they too had been sent away; now they must not repeat that by trusting their prophets (verses 8-9, 20).

decisions.choice: rising early and sending (Literal); again and again (Balanced); over and over (Readable)
decisions.reason: The wording set for this phrase throughout Jeremiah. "Servants" is kept at every level for the prophets, as in 7:25.

decisions.choice: you exiles; with my message
decisions.reason: Readable says who "you" are (m3) and what the prophets brought.

pieces: But you, all you exiles whom I sent away from Jerusalem to Babylon, hear the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

L.20: And you, hear the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, all the exiles whom I sent away from Jerusalem to Babylon.

R.20: So now, all of you captives whom I sent away from Jerusalem to Babylon, listen to the message from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: and you: an emphatic turn to the exiles
decisions.reason: The pronoun is written out: "as for you". Unlike those who would not listen (verse 19), the exiles are called to hear now; the word they are to hear follows in verses 21-23.

decisions.choice: whom I sent away: a gentler word than "exiled"
decisions.reason: The verb means to send off or let go. It is used of the exiles in 24:5, and it again makes God the one who sent them.

decisions.choice: the address first, then the command
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the long address before "hear", as English does. Readable says "So now" to mark the turn.

records.source: כֹּֽה־אָמַר֩ יְהוָ֨ה צְבָא֜וֹת אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל אֶל־אַחְאָ֤ב בֶּן־קֽוֹלָיָה֙ וְאֶל־צִדְקִיָּ֣הוּ בֶן־מַֽעֲשֵׂיָ֔ה הַֽנִּבְּאִ֥ים לָכֶ֛ם בִּשְׁמִ֖י שָׁ֑קֶר הִנְנִ֣י׀נֹתֵ֣ן אֹתָ֗ם בְּיַד֙ נְבֽוּכַדְרֶאצַּ֣ר מֶֽלֶךְ־בָּבֶ֔ל וְהִכָּ֖ם לְעֵינֵיכֶֽם׃
records.gloss: Thus says Yahweh of hosts, [the] God of Israel, concerning Ahab son of Kolaiah and concerning Zedekiah son of Maaseiah, the [ones] prophesying to you in my name falsehood: Behold, I [am] giving them into [the] hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, and he will strike them before your eyes.
pieces: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies, the God of Israel, says this about Ahab son of Kolaiah and about Zedekiah son of Maaseiah, who are prophesying lies to you in {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name: I am about to hand them over to Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, and he will put them to death before your eyes.

L.21: Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of hosts, the God of Israel, concerning Ahab son of Kolaiah and concerning Zedekiah son of Maaseiah, who are prophesying a lie to you in {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name: Look, I am giving them into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, and he will strike them down before your eyes.

R.21: This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies, the God of Israel, says about Ahab son of Kolaiah and about Zedekiah son of Maaseiah. They are using {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name to tell you lies. I am going to hand them over to Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, and he will kill them while you watch.

decisions.choice: Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah: two prophets among the exiles
decisions.reason: These two men are known only from this passage. This Zedekiah is not the king of verse 3; the name was common. They were among the prophets in Babylon of verse 15.

decisions.choice: Nebuchadrezzar: the form of the name with r
decisions.reason: Verses 1 and 3 spell the king's name Nebuchadnezzar; this verse has the form Nebuchadrezzar used in most of Jeremiah (see 25:1). It is the same king.

decisions.choice: giving them into the hand of: handing them over to the power of
decisions.reason: To give someone into another's hand is to put that person in the other's power, here for punishment (21:7; 22:25).

decisions.choice: he will strike them: he will put them to death
decisions.reason: The verb means to strike, and often to kill. Verse 22 says how they died. The text does not say why the king of Babylon would execute them; prophets who promised a quick end to Babylon's rule (verses 8-9; 28:2-4) could well be seen as stirring up revolt. Verse 23 gives God's reason.

decisions.choice: Nebuchadrezzar
decisions.reason: Each verse keeps the form of the name its Hebrew uses (m2).

decisions.choice: hand them over; put them to death (Balanced); kill them while you watch (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the idioms mean in plain English (m3, m4).

records.source: וְלֻקַּ֤ח מֵהֶם֙ קְלָלָ֔ה לְכֹל֙ גָּל֣וּת יְהוּדָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר בְּבָבֶ֖ל לֵאמֹ֑ר יְשִֽׂמְךָ֤ יְהוָה֙ כְּצִדְקִיָּ֣הוּ וּכְאֶחָ֔ב אֲשֶׁר־קָלָ֥ם מֶֽלֶךְ־בָּבֶ֖ל בָּאֵֽשׁ׃
records.gloss: And will be taken from them a curse by all [the] exile of Judah who [are] in Babylon, saying: May make you Yahweh like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom roasted them [the] king of Babylon in the fire,
pieces: Their fate will become a curse that all the exiles of Judah in Babylon will use: 'May {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} make you like Zedekiah and Ahab, the men the king of Babylon roasted alive in the fire,'

L.22: And from them a curse will be taken up by all the exiles of Judah who [are] in Babylon, saying, 'May {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} make you like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire,'

R.22: All the captives from Judah who are in Babylon will use their names when they curse someone. They will say, 'May {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} make you end up like Zedekiah and Ahab, who were burned to death by the king of Babylon!'

decisions.choice: a curse ... roasted: a play on words
decisions.reason: The word for "curse" (qelalah) sounds like the verb "roasted" (qalah), and both echo the name of Ahab's father, Kolaiah. The men's very fate becomes the curse people speak.

decisions.choice: roasted in the fire: burned to death, a Babylonian punishment
decisions.reason: Babylonian law named burning as the penalty for some crimes, and Daniel 3 tells of a furnace used to put men to death (Daniel 3:6, 19-23). The two prophets were burned alive.

decisions.choice: a curse will be taken from them: their fate will be used as a curse
decisions.reason: People will take the two men as the pattern for a curse: "may you end up like them". It is what 24:9 and verse 18 mean by a people becoming "a curse" (compare Isaiah 65:15).

decisions.choice: single quotation marks; the sentence runs on into verse 23
decisions.reason: The curse is quoted inside the letter, so it takes single marks. Literal and Balanced end with a comma, since verse 23 gives the reason; Readable ends the sentence here.

decisions.choice: roasted alive (Balanced); burned to death (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced adds "alive" and Readable says plainly what "roasted in the fire" meant (m2); both leave out the second "like", which English does not need.

records.source: יַ֡עַן אֲשֶׁר֩ עָשׂ֨וּ נְבָלָ֜ה בְּיִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל וַיְנַֽאֲפוּ֙ אֶת־נְשֵׁ֣י רֵֽעֵיהֶ֔ם וַיְדַבְּר֨וּ דָבָ֤ר בִּשְׁמִי֙ שֶׁ֔קֶר אֲשֶׁ֖ר ל֣וֹא צִוִּיתִ֑ם וְאָנֹכִ֛י הַיּוֹדֵ֥עַוָעֵ֖ד נְאֻם־יְהוָֽה׃ס
records.gloss: because that they did folly in Israel, and they committed adultery with [the] wives of their neighbors, and they spoke a word in my name [of] falsehood, which not I commanded them; and I [am] the [one] knowing and witness, declaration of Yahweh.
pieces: because they have done a disgraceful thing in Israel. They have committed adultery with their neighbors' wives and have spoken lies in {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name, words I did not command them to speak. I am the one who knows it, and I am witness to it, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}."

L.23: because they have done an outrage in Israel, and they have committed adultery with their neighbors' wives, and they have spoken in {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name a lying word, which I did not command them; and I [am] the one who knows, and [I am] witness, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}."

R.23: This will happen because they have done shameful things in Israel. They have slept with other men's wives. And they have told lies and said that the messages came from {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, when I never told them to say anything. I know all about it, and I am a witness to it, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}."

decisions.choice: the one who knows: the form read aloud
decisions.reason: The written consonants (ketiv) can be read "he knows"; the scribes marked "the one who knows" to be read aloud (qere). Both say that God himself knows what they have done.

decisions.choice: an outrage: a shameful act that breaks the bonds of the community
decisions.reason: The word names a deed so gross that it disgraces the whole people, often a sexual crime (Genesis 34:7; Deuteronomy 22:21; Judges 20:6, 10) or a breach of what is holy (Joshua 7:15). "In Israel" means among God's people.

decisions.choice: adultery with their neighbors' wives: a breach of the commandments
decisions.reason: The law forbade adultery and desire for a neighbor's wife (Exodus 20:14, 17). Jeremiah had charged the prophets of Jerusalem with the same sin (23:14).

decisions.choice: I am the one who knows and the witness
decisions.reason: In a court a witness testifies to what he has seen. God himself has seen what these men did, even if it was hidden from others, and he will testify against them (compare Malachi 3:5; Micah 1:2).

decisions.choice: a closing quotation mark
decisions.reason: The letter that began in verse 4 ends here.

decisions.choice: slept with other men's wives; told lies and said that the messages came from me
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what adultery is and what speaking lies in God's name means. "I never told them to say anything" gives "which I did not command them".

records.source: וְאֶל־שְׁמַעְיָ֥הוּ הַנֶּחֱלָמִ֖י תֹּאמַ֥ר לֵאמֹֽר׃
records.gloss: And to Shemaiah the Nehelamite you will say, saying:
pieces: "To Shemaiah the Nehelamite you are to say:

L.24: "And to Shemaiah the Nehelamite you shall say, saying:

R.24: "Give this message to Shemaiah the Nehelamite:

decisions.choice: and to Shemaiah you shall say: God now speaks to Jeremiah
decisions.reason: A new section starts without an introduction. The "you" is singular: God tells Jeremiah what to say to Shemaiah, a prophet among the exiles who had written to Jerusalem in reply to Jeremiah's letter. The speech is broken off at verse 28 and finished in verses 31-32.

decisions.choice: the Nehelamite: of an unknown place or family
decisions.reason: The word names where Shemaiah or his family came from, but no place called Nehelam is known. It sounds like the word for "dream", and some think it may be a nickname for a man who trusted dreams (verse 8), but this cannot be shown.

decisions.choice: an opening quotation mark
decisions.reason: God's words to Jeremiah are quoted from here to verse 28. The message to Shemaiah inside them takes single marks, his letter double marks again, and the words he quotes from Jeremiah single marks.

decisions.choice: Give this message to
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what "you shall say, saying" means.

records.heading: A message for Shemaiah

records.source: כֹּֽה־אָמַ֞ר יְהוָ֧ה צְבָא֛וֹת אֱלֹהֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לֵאמֹ֑ר יַ֡עַן אֲשֶׁ֣ר אַתָּה֩ שָׁלַ֨חְתָּ בְשִׁמְכָ֜ה סְפָרִ֗ים אֶל־כָּל־הָעָם֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בִּירוּשָׁלִַ֔ם וְאֶל־צְפַנְיָ֤ה בֶן־מַֽעֲשֵׂיָה֙ הַכֹּהֵ֔ן וְאֶ֥ל כָּל־הַכֹּהֲנִ֖ים לֵאמֹֽר׃
records.gloss: Thus says Yahweh of hosts, [the] God of Israel, saying: Because that you sent in your name letters to all the people who [are] in Jerusalem, and to Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest, and to all the priests, saying:
pieces: '{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies, the God of Israel, says this: You sent letters in your own name to all the people in Jerusalem, to Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest and to all the priests. You wrote:

L.25: 'Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of hosts, the God of Israel, saying: Because you have sent letters in your own name to all the people who [are] in Jerusalem, and to Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest, and to all the priests, saying,

R.25: 'This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies, the God of Israel, says: You sent letters in your own name to all the people in Jerusalem. You sent them to Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest and to all the other priests. You wrote:

decisions.choice: because you sent: a sentence left unfinished
decisions.reason: The sentence begins "because" but never reaches its "therefore". The quotation of Shemaiah's letter runs on to verse 28, and the judgment comes only in verses 31-32, where "because ... therefore" is spoken in full.

decisions.choice: in your own name: on your own authority
decisions.reason: The other prophets spoke falsely "in my name" (verses 9, 21, 23). Shemaiah wrote in his own name, giving orders to the priests in Jerusalem without any word from God.

decisions.choice: Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest: the second-ranking priest in the temple
decisions.reason: Zephaniah was the "second priest", next to the chief priest (52:24), and King Zedekiah twice sent him to ask Jeremiah for a word from the LORD (21:1; 37:3). He was put to death by the Babylonians after Jerusalem fell (52:24-27).

decisions.choice: You sent letters ... You wrote:
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable state the charge without "because", since the sentence it begins is not finished (m1), and say "You wrote" for "saying". Readable breaks the verse into short sentences.

records.source: יְהוָ֞ה נְתָנְךָ֣ כֹהֵ֗ן תַּ֚חַת יְהוֹיָדָ֣ע הַכֹּהֵ֔ן לִֽהְי֤וֹת פְּקִדִים֙ בֵּ֣ית יְהוָ֔ה לְכָל־אִ֥ישׁ מְשֻׁגָּ֖ע וּמִתְנַבֵּ֑א וְנָתַתָּ֥ה אֹת֛וֹ אֶל־הַמַּהְפֶּ֖כֶת וְאֶל־הַצִּינֹֽק׃
records.gloss: Yahweh has made you priest instead of Jehoiada the priest, to be overseers [in the] house of Yahweh for every man [who is] mad and acting the prophet, and you will put him into the stocks and into the collar.
pieces: "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has made you priest in place of Jehoiada the priest, so that there would be officers in the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} to deal with any madman who sets himself up as a prophet. You should put such a man in the stocks and the neck irons.

L.26: "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has made you priest in place of Jehoiada the priest, to be overseers in the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} over every man who is mad and acts the prophet, and you are to put him in the stocks and in the collar.

R.26: "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} made you priest in place of Jehoiada the priest. You are in charge in the temple of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. You are supposed to watch for any crazy person who acts like a prophet. You should lock him in the stocks with an iron collar around his neck.

decisions.choice: Jehoiada the priest: probably the priest who guarded the temple for young King Joash
decisions.reason: Jehoiada led the overthrow of Queen Athaliah and set guards over the house of the LORD (2 Kings 11:4-18). Shemaiah may name him as the model of a priest who kept order in the temple, or he may mean a later priest of that name, perhaps Zephaniah's predecessor, of whom nothing else is known.

decisions.choice: to be overseers: the priest and the officers under him
decisions.reason: The noun is plural. Zephaniah and the priests with him are to be the temple's officers. Pashhur had held this office of overseer when he put Jeremiah in the stocks (20:1-2).

decisions.choice: mad and acting the prophet: a sneer at prophets
decisions.reason: The first word means insane, raving. It was used in scorn of prophets (2 Kings 9:11; Hosea 9:7). The verb form for "prophesy" can describe raving behavior (1 Samuel 18:10). Shemaiah means any wild man who claims to speak for God.

decisions.choice: the stocks and the collar: devices for holding a prisoner
decisions.reason: The stocks are the device in which Pashhur held Jeremiah (20:2). The second word is found only here. It may name a collar or iron band for the neck; some take it as a narrow cell.

decisions.choice: double quotation marks for Shemaiah's letter
decisions.reason: Shemaiah's letter is quoted inside the LORD's message to him, which is quoted inside the LORD's words to Jeremiah, so it takes double marks again.

decisions.choice: sets himself up as a prophet, neck irons (Balanced); acts like a prophet, iron collar (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable bring out the scorn in the verb (m3) and say what the collar was. Readable says "crazy person" for the madman and begins new sentences.

records.source: וְעַתָּ֗ה לָ֚מָּה לֹ֣א גָעַ֔רְתָּ בְּיִרְמְיָ֖הוּ הָֽעֲנְּתֹתִ֑י הַמִּתְנַבֵּ֖א לָכֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And now, why not you rebuked Jeremiah the Anathothite, the [one] acting the prophet to you?
pieces: So why have you not rebuked Jeremiah of Anathoth, who sets himself up as a prophet among you?

L.27: And now, why have you not rebuked Jeremiah of Anathoth, who acts the prophet to you?

R.27: So why have you not done anything about Jeremiah from Anathoth? He is acting like a prophet among you.

decisions.choice: rebuked: reprimanded and restrained
decisions.reason: The verb means to rebuke sharply, and so to check or restrain. Shemaiah wants Zephaniah to use his authority against Jeremiah, as verse 26 says.

decisions.choice: Jeremiah of Anathoth: the prophet named by his home village
decisions.reason: Anathoth was a town of priests a few miles north of Jerusalem, Jeremiah's home (1:1; 11:21-23). Naming him by his village, not as a prophet, may be meant to belittle him.

decisions.choice: who acts the prophet: the same verb form as in verse 26
decisions.reason: Shemaiah uses the word he used for the madman, so he counts Jeremiah among them.

decisions.choice: sets himself up as a prophet (Balanced); acting like a prophet (Readable); among you
decisions.reason: As in verse 26. Balanced and Readable say "among you", since Jeremiah prophesied in Jerusalem, where Zephaniah was.

records.source: כִּ֣י עַל־כֵּ֞ן שָׁלַ֥ח אֵלֵ֛ינוּ בָּבֶ֥ל לֵאמֹ֖ר אֲרֻכָּ֣ה הִ֑יא בְּנ֤וּ בָתִּים֙ וְשֵׁ֔בוּ וְנִטְע֣וּ גַנּ֔וֹת וְאִכְל֖וּ אֶת־פְּרִיהֶֽן׃
records.gloss: For therefore he has sent to us [to] Babylon, saying: Long [is] it; build houses and dwell, and plant gardens and eat their produce.
pieces: For he has even sent word to us in Babylon, saying, 'It will be a long time. Build houses and settle down in them. Plant gardens and eat what they produce.'"'"

L.28: For therefore he has sent to us [in] Babylon, saying, 'It [will be] long; build houses and live [in them], and plant gardens and eat their produce.'"'"

R.28: He has even sent a message to us in Babylon. He told us that we will be here a long time, and that we should build houses and live in them, and plant gardens and eat the food they grow."'"

decisions.choice: for therefore: "for he has even" or "for this reason"
alternatives: for that is why he sent to us
decisions.reason: The words are literally "for therefore". They may stress how far Jeremiah has gone ("he has even sent to us"), or say that because no one stopped him he has been able to send his letter. The point is the same: Shemaiah treats the letter as proof that Jeremiah must be silenced.

decisions.choice: it will be long; build houses ...: Shemaiah quotes Jeremiah's letter
decisions.reason: Shemaiah quotes verse 5 and sums up verse 10 as "it will be long". The word for long is feminine, and its subject is not named; the exile, or the time of waiting, is meant.

decisions.choice: the end of Shemaiah's letter and of the LORD's broken-off speech
decisions.reason: The quotation of Shemaiah's letter ends here. The message the LORD began in verse 25 is not finished; verse 29 goes back to the story, and verses 31-32 give the judgment.

decisions.choice: indirect speech
decisions.reason: Readable reports Jeremiah's words in Shemaiah's letter without a further set of quotation marks, which would be hard to follow. The meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: closing quotation marks
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced close Jeremiah's words, Shemaiah's letter, the LORD's message and the LORD's words to Jeremiah, in that order; Readable has one set fewer (r-en-1).

records.gloss: And read Zephaniah the priest the letter the this in [the] ears of Jeremiah the prophet.
pieces: Zephaniah the priest read this letter aloud to Jeremiah the prophet.

L.29: And Zephaniah the priest read this letter in the ears of Jeremiah the prophet.

R.29: Zephaniah the priest read the letter out loud to Jeremiah the prophet.

decisions.choice: the story resumes
decisions.reason: The narrator tells what happened when Shemaiah's letter reached Jerusalem. The LORD's word about Shemaiah in verses 24-28 and 30-32 was given to Jeremiah after this.

decisions.choice: Zephaniah read the letter to Jeremiah
decisions.reason: Instead of putting Jeremiah in the stocks as Shemaiah demanded, Zephaniah read him the letter. The text does not say why: he may have been warning Jeremiah, or giving him a chance to answer. Zephaniah was the priest Zedekiah sent to Jeremiah to ask for his prayers (21:1; 37:3).

decisions.choice: in the ears of: aloud to
decisions.reason: To read "in someone's ears" is to read aloud so that he hears (36:6, 10).

decisions.choice: aloud to (Balanced); out loud to (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the idiom means (m3).

records.source: וַֽיְהִי֙ דְּבַר־יְהוָ֔ה אֶֽל־יִרְמְיָ֖הוּ לֵאמֹֽר׃
records.gloss: And came [the] word of Yahweh to Jeremiah, saying:
pieces: Then the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} came to Jeremiah:

L.30: And the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} came to Jeremiah, saying:

R.30: Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} gave Jeremiah this message:

decisions.choice: then the word came: after Zephaniah read the letter
decisions.reason: The LORD answered Shemaiah through Jeremiah once the letter had been read to him. Verses 24-28 and 31-32 belong to this word.

decisions.choice: the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah, saying: (Literal); ... came to Jeremiah: (Balanced); the LORD gave Jeremiah this message: (Readable)
decisions.reason: The wording set for "the word of the LORD came to me" in Jeremiah, with Jeremiah's name.

decisions.choice: because ...: the charge, now spoken in full
decisions.reason: This takes up the unfinished "because" of verse 25 and goes on to the "therefore" of verse 32.

decisions.choice: I did not send him, and he has made you trust in a lie
decisions.reason: The same words were spoken to Hananiah, who broke the yoke from Jeremiah's neck: "the LORD has not sent you, and you have made this people trust in a lie" (28:15). Shemaiah, like Hananiah, is a prophet God did not send.

decisions.choice: has prophesied to you: in his letter
decisions.reason: Shemaiah's letter claimed to speak for God ("the LORD has made you priest", verse 26). This counts as prophesying, though God had not sent him.

decisions.choice: God's words to Jeremiah in double marks, the message to the exiles in single marks
decisions.reason: The message Jeremiah is to send is quoted inside God's words to him, as in 7:2. Readable ends the sentence here and starts verse 32 with "So".

records.gloss: therefore thus says Yahweh: Behold, I [am] visiting upon Shemaiah the Nehelamite and upon his offspring; not will be to him a man dwelling in [the] midst of the people the this, and not he will see the good that I [am] doing for my people, declaration of Yahweh, for rebellion he has spoken against Yahweh.
pieces: therefore {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says this: I am about to punish Shemaiah the Nehelamite and his descendants. No one of his line will be left living among this people, and he will not see the good that I am going to do for {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} people, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, because he has preached rebellion against {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.'"

L.32: therefore thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: Look, I am visiting [punishment] on Shemaiah the Nehelamite and on his offspring. He will not have anyone living among this people, and he will not see the good that I am doing for {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} people, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, for he has spoken rebellion against {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.'"

R.32: So this is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says: I will punish Shemaiah the Nehelamite and his descendants. None of his family will be left among this people. He will not live to see the good things I am going to do for {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} people, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. This is because he has told people to turn against {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.'"

decisions.choice: I am visiting on: I will punish
decisions.reason: The verb that in verse 10 meant God's coming to help means here, with "on", his coming to punish.

decisions.choice: he will not have anyone dwelling among this people: his family line will be cut off
decisions.reason: No descendant of his will be among God's people when they are restored. He promised a quick return and will have no share in the real one.

decisions.choice: the good that I am doing for my people: the restoration promised in verses 10-14
decisions.reason: The "good" is the "good word" of verse 10: the return from exile. The participle describes God's plan as already under way.

decisions.choice: he has spoken rebellion against the LORD: the charge against a false prophet
decisions.reason: The law says that a prophet who speaks rebellion against the LORD is to die (Deuteronomy 13:6), and Jeremiah used these words of Hananiah (28:16).

decisions.choice: punish (Balanced, Readable); preached rebellion (Balanced); told people to turn against (Readable)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "visiting" and brackets the punishment it implies; Balanced and Readable say "punish". "Spoken rebellion" means urging people to turn from the LORD.

decisions.choice: closing quotation marks
decisions.reason: The message to the exiles and the LORD's words to Jeremiah both end here.
